messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Emily was nineteen when the night that shattered her sense of safety unfolded. After a celebration at a local bar, she walked the winding streets home, her ears still ringing from the loud conversations inside. A motorcycle’s sudden revving burst across the quiet alley, and a man’s voice rose in harsh Arabic, shouting and thrusting a knife at her. The blow landed hard against her shoulder, the world collapsing into a blur of pain and the smell of burnt gasoline. The very sound of a motorcycle, the foreign language she could barely catch, and the acrid scent of spilled alcohol became the triggers that would haunt her in the days that followed. From that instant, Emily began to steer clear of any evening when a motorcycle might pass, of any moment that might echo the man's Arabic cries, and of the brief, involuntary scent of alcohol that lingered in her own apartment after visiting friends. She stopped watching her own reflection in mirrors, believing that her eyes might betray her vulnerability. The assault not only left a physical scar but also shattered the certainty she had once held that the world was orderly and that she was capable of navigating it. She convinced herself that someone else—someone more able—could have stopped the attack. The memory of that night clung to Emily like a second skin. She described how, without warning, a single noise—a distant motorcycle engine—would transport her back to the instant the knife had cut her. When she tried to recall the assault, she could hear the hiss of the engine in her mind and smell the sharp, metallic scent of blood, as if the event were replaying itself. These involuntary intrusions set off a state of constant threat monitoring; she was perpetually listening for unfamiliar sounds, checking behind her as if an unseen pursuer could appear from any direction. Each flashback amplified her sense of danger, which in turn deepened her memory of the assault, creating a tight loop of threat and recollection. The ongoing sense of threat pushed her to believe that her own safety was fragile, reinforcing her negative appraisals that she had lost her capability and that others would have been able to prevent the tragedy. In turn, these appraisals fed her fear, making her vigilance even more pronounced. Her avoidance strategies compounded the cycle: by refusing to be outside at night, she cut herself off from normal routines, heightening her sense that the world was hostile; by avoiding anniversaries of the date she had been attacked, she kept the memory fresh, and by refusing to notice her own body, she missed signs that might have signaled her distress, which kept her memory alive and her fear unrelieved. The avoidance behaviors also served to remind her of the trigger moments—motorcycle horns and the smell of alcohol—thereby tightening the web of cause and effect. In the weeks that followed, Emily’s life became increasingly constrained. She no longer volunteered at the local community center, a job she had loved before the assault, because it required her to be in crowds where she feared she might hear a motorcycle or a shout. When her husband, who has been her anchor, asked if she wanted to celebrate their anniversary together, she declined, citing that the date would bring back painful memories. The apartment, which once felt like a sanctuary, now felt like a trap, and her refusal to confront her own body left her feeling perpetually detached. Each time she avoided a trigger, a memory surfaced, prompting her to re-avoid, and each avoidance reinforced her negative belief that she could not regain control. The pattern was relentless: triggers led her to evade, evasion kept memories alive, memories heightened threat perception, threat magnified negative appraisals, and negative appraisals drove her further into avoidance. It was the accumulation of these loops, coupled with a growing isolation from friends and a loss of self-confidence, that finally pushed Emily to seek help. She now tells her therapist that the most terrifying thought is the possibility that another day might bring the same sensory storm—motorcycle noise, harsh Arabic, the scent of alcohol—and that she will be forced to relive the assault again. Yet she also holds a fragile hope that with guidance she might dismantle the cycle, reclaim her sense of safety, and find a way to look at herself in the mirror without feeling watched. The decision to come forward reflects a dawning belief that she can, once again, be capable of navigating her world without being haunted by that one terrible night.
